subject: HealPilot: model selection, long-context behavior & next steps

Subject: Follow-up + sample data (long-context requirements)

Hi Hannah / Rishi / Marissa —

Thanks again for the demo today — that was really helpful. A quick recap from our side: HealPilot is building an encounter-summarization product that needs to reliably summarize multi-hour telehealth transcripts and up to ~25 pages of attachments aggregated per patient (so roughly 12k–18k tokens in some cases). Main asks from the call:

- Recommendations on a model family / quantization profile that balances fidelity for clinical summarization with reasonable latency/cost.
- Concrete eval plan: prompt sets, summarization metrics, and truncation/regression checks.
- A quick pilot idea (canary) to validate truncation behavior and hallucination rate on real notes.

I attached a short call recording and a zip with three de-identified encounter notes (sample_patient_notes.zip) to help seed the evaluation.

Can you share an initial recommendation and an outline of next steps by Monday? We’d like to present a plan to our CTO on Tuesday.

—Emma
Emma Rhodes

emma@healpilot.ai | +1-415-555-0132

From: hannah_schmitt <hannah@redwood.ai>

Cc: marissa_cole <marissa@redwood.ai>, rishi_malhotra <rishi@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Follow-up + sample data (long-context requirements)

Emma —

Great talking yesterday, and thanks for the samples. High-level answers and a proposed evaluation approach below. I kept it concise so your CTO can scan it quickly.

1) Short model recommendations (first-pass)
- rwdx-16k (FP16) — best balance for fidelity on long clinical documents, strong summarization precision.
- rwdx-64k-cascade (quantized q4_0) — for the tail of extremely long notes; we route long requests to a cascade that does chunked summarization + merge to avoid blind truncation.
- rwdx-13b-llama-compat-q4 — a lower-cost option for nearline processing where latency is less critical.

2) Why these:
- We prioritize models with larger context and robust attention kernel selection. The cascade approach reduces hallucination risk versus naive truncation by summarizing in-window then merging summaries with a second-pass model.

3) Proposed eval plan (deliverables / timeline)
- Day 0–2: Ingest your ZIP and run a 20-doc smoke test (sanity checks, token counts, quick latency samples).
- Day 3–7: Full bench: run summarization prompts (see attached planned_eval_prompts.csv) across the three model options above. Metrics: rouge-l, bleu-lite (for structure), length-preservation, factuality score (entity-precision), and hallucination rate by entity type.
- Day 8–10: Truncation stress tests: synthetic prefix shifts, shifting salient info towards tail, and chunk-merge evaluation.
- Day 11–14: Pilot proposal: 500 notes/1000 summary cycles on dedicated reserved capacity (1–2 gpus) to validate production latency/cost and edge-case hallucinations.

Benchmarks & links: 
- Initial benchmark (internal): https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/long-context/2026/healpilot
- Shared drive with prompts and expected output schema: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/healpilot-eval

4) Risks & mitigations
- Truncation can silently drop key entities — we recommend the cascade/merge flow and a strict QA pass on entity recall.
- Quantization may slightly reduce entity recall for rarer medical terms — we’ll A/B full-precision on a small sample to measure delta.

Next steps / ask from you by Monday: confirm the three sample patient notes are representative, and share 20 more (de-identified) if possible so we can accelerate the Day 0–2 smoke test. Also tell us your preferred pilot start window (Nov 16–30 looks open on our side).

I’ve attached the planned_eval_prompts.csv with an initial set of prompts and scoring rubrics.

Thanks —
Hannah Schmitt
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
H: +1-612-555-0188

Attachments: planned_eval_prompts.csv

Subject: Re: Follow-up + sample data (long-context requirements)

Emma / team —

Quick technical notes to add to Hannah’s plan:

- Truncation behavior: if you feed a ~15k token doc directly to a 16k-context model that also needs room for generation, you’ll hit practical limits once you factor in the output window. Our cascade approach does: chunk (sliding window with 1k overlap) → local chunk summarizer (rwdx-16k qfp16) → merge-phase with a low-temp pass to stitch and fact-check. This reduces input truncation windows while keeping generation costs bounded.

- KV cache and continuous conversation: for multi-session patient history, keep patient KV-cache keys per encounter; avoid warming full history on every request. We can provide a small KV management helper as part of the pilot.

- Quantization tradeoffs: q4_0 looks good for cost-sensitive runs; q2/q3 can save more compute but we’ve seen entity recall drop ~3–6% for low-frequency medical terminology. We should A/B test 200 documents to quantify.

- Cost estimate (ballpark for pilot): 500 notes processed end-to-end on reserved capacity (rwdx-16k FP16 primary + rwdx-64k-cascade fallback) — ~ $12k–$18k over a two-week pilot (includes infra and engineer time).

Happy to spin up the smoke test once you confirm sample representativeness.

—Marissa
Marissa Cole
Principal Applied ML Engineer, Redwood Inference
